claims.text: The baseline consists of untreated Pt nanoparticles with native surface states and no oxidation-altering pretreatment.
O2 plasma pretreatment will induce controlled surface oxidation on Pt nanoparticles.
Moderate surface oxidation forms a thin, stabilized PtOx layer on the nanoparticles.
A PtOx surface layer changes the adsorption energies of ethanol and its oxidized intermediates.
Modified intermediate adsorption facilitates the electron- and proton-transfer steps of ethanol oxidation.
Complete ethanol oxidation is a 12-electron process.
Moderate Pt surface oxidation lowers the overpotential or onset potential for complete ethanol oxidation.
Moderately oxidized Pt nanoparticles will have a higher steady-state ethanol-oxidation current than untreated Pt nanoparticles.
The PtOx layer acts as a barrier that protects the Pt core and reduces Pt dissolution.
Reduced Pt dissolution enhances catalyst durability.
Excessive surface oxidation impedes ethanol-oxidation activity.
The hypothesized effect should be significant in acidic electrolyte at 0.2–0.7 V versus RHE.
Alkaline electrolyte or extreme potentials may destabilize PtOx and alter catalytic behavior.
Operando XPS or Raman spectroscopy can monitor the formation, evolution, and stability of PtOx during ethanol oxidation.
Comparing plasma-treated and untreated Pt under otherwise identical acidic electrochemical conditions isolates the effect of the pretreatment.
Failure of PtOx formation or stability to correlate with lower onset potential and improved durability would falsify the proposed causal role.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that excessive oxidation will impede activity, but the falsification rule treats excessive oxidation without catalytic enhancement as evidence against the hypothesis. That observation is consistent with the stated prediction and therefore cannot by itself falsify the proposed benefit of moderate oxidation.
